topics.DFA: DFU: definition, pathophysiology, risk factors, examination & classification

cards.q: How does the Malaysian CPG define a diabetic foot ulcer (diabetic foot)?
cards.a:
• **Infection, ulceration or destruction** of tissues of the foot
• associated with **neuropathy and/or peripheral arterial disease (PAD)**
• in a person with **diabetes mellitus**
cards.m: Three verbs (infect, ulcerate, destroy) + two causes (nerves, arteries) + one disease (DM).

cards.q: What are the three pathophysiological pillars of diabetic foot ulceration?
cards.a:
• **Neuropathy** - sensory, motor, autonomic
• **Vasculopathy** - peripheral arterial disease (macro- and microvascular)
• **Immunopathy** - impaired host defence, so infection spreads fast
cards.m: The diabetic foot: **can't feel it, can't feed it, can't fight it**.

cards.q: How does sensory neuropathy lead to a foot ulcer?
cards.a:
• **Loss of protective sensation** - pain no longer warns of injury
• Repetitive unnoticed trauma: tight shoes, stones/foreign bodies in the shoe, burns
• Ulcer forms at **high-pressure points** and is ignored until infected
cards.m: Pain is the foot's burglar alarm - neuropathy cuts the wire.

cards.q: How does motor neuropathy contribute to diabetic foot ulceration?
cards.a:
• Weakness of **intrinsic foot muscles** -> long flexors/extensors unopposed
• **Claw/hammer toes** with prominent **metatarsal heads** (fat pad pulled forward)
• Raised plantar pressure -> **callus** -> ulcer beneath the callus
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: callus over a metatarsal head is a pre-ulcer - pare it.

cards.q: What are the effects of autonomic neuropathy on the diabetic foot?
cards.a:
• Loss of sweating (**anhidrosis**) -> dry, cracked, fissured skin = portal for bacteria
• **Arteriovenous shunting** -> warm foot, distended dorsal veins, bounding pulses
• Increased bone blood flow -> osteopenia, a basis for **Charcot foot**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: a warm, dry, cracked foot with good pulses is still a high-risk foot.

cards.q: What is the vascular (vasculopathy) contribution to diabetic foot ulcers?
cards.a:
• **Peripheral arterial disease** - atherosclerosis, typically distal (infrapopliteal/tibial) vessels
• Plus **microvascular** dysfunction
• Ischaemia -> poor wound healing, poor antibiotic delivery, gangrene
cards.m: No blood, no healing - and no antibiotic reaches the bug.

cards.q: Why do infections spread rapidly in the diabetic foot (immunopathy)?
cards.a:
• Hyperglycaemia impairs **neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis and intracellular killing**
• Inflammatory signs are often **blunted** (neuropathy + ischaemia)
• So deep infection can be advanced before it is obvious
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: in diabetics, a mild-looking foot can hide a deep abscess - always probe and image.

cards.q: List the SYSTEMIC risk factors for diabetic foot ulcer given in the lecture.
cards.a:
• **Poor glycaemic control**
• **Cigarette smoking**
• **Diabetic nephropathy**
• **Visual impairment**
cards.m: Sugar, Smoke, Kidneys, Eyes.

cards.q: List the LOCAL risk factors for diabetic foot ulcer.
cards.a:
• **Previous ulceration**
• **Previous amputation**
• **Peripheral vascular disease and neuropathy**
• **Foot deformity**
• **Infection**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: a previous ulcer or amputation is the strongest predictor of a new ulcer.

cards.q: Why is visual impairment a risk factor for diabetic foot ulcer?
cards.a:
• Patient cannot **inspect their own feet** daily
• Small wounds, blisters and foreign bodies go unnoticed (especially with neuropathy)
• Needs a carer to check feet and closer clinic monitoring
cards.m: Neuropathy removes the pain warning; blindness removes the visual warning.

cards.q: What are the clinical presentations of the diabetic foot listed in the lecture?
cards.a:
• **Foot ulcer**
• **Infection**
• **Callus / hyperkeratosis**
• **Cold** (ischaemic) or **warm** (neuropathic/Charcot) extremities
• **Gangrene**
• **Charcot foot**

cards.q: Neuropathic vs ischaemic diabetic foot ulcer - how do you tell them apart?
cards.a:
• **Neuropathic**: plantar pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel), **painless**, punched-out with **callus rim**, warm foot, **pulses present**
• **Ischaemic**: toe tips / foot margins, **painful**, pale sloughy base, cold foot, **absent pulses**, delayed CRT
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Neuropathic = Numb, warm, under pressure. Ischaemic = Insults the toe tips, cold, hurts.

cards.q: In the diabetic foot examination, what should general inspection and footwear inspection include?
cards.a:
• Introduce, consent, expose to **at least mid-thigh** (respect modesty)
• **Gait** assessment
• **Footwear**: abnormal wear pattern, materials/foreign bodies inside the shoe, **remove and review insoles**
cards.m: The shoe is the crime scene - inspect it as carefully as the foot.

cards.q: Which pulses and perfusion sign are checked in the diabetic foot examination, and what is normal CRT?
cards.a:
• **Femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, dorsalis pedis** arteries
• **Capillary refill time** normal **< 2 seconds**; > 2 s suggests poor circulation
cards.m: Work from groin to foot: F-P-PT-DP.

cards.q: What does the Semmes-Weinstein monofilament test detect and how is it performed?
cards.a:
• Detects **loss of protective sensation** (LOPS)
• **10 g** nylon monofilament pressed **perpendicular until it buckles** (~1-2 s)
• 10 plantar sites: hallux, 1st/3rd/5th metatarsal heads, medial and lateral midfoot, medial and lateral heel, 1st and 5th toe pulps
• Avoid callus, ulcers and scars
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: if the patient cannot feel 10 g, he cannot feel a stone in his shoe.

cards.q: Apart from the monofilament, which other sensory tests are part of the diabetic foot examination?
cards.a:
• **Vibration** with a **128 Hz tuning fork** on a distal bony prominence (e.g. hallux IP joint)
• **Glove-and-stocking** sensory loss (pinprick/light touch)
• **Proprioception** (big toe joint position)
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: vibration and proprioception (large fibres) are often lost early - 128 Hz, not 512 Hz.

cards.q: What does the motor/musculoskeletal and reflex part of the diabetic foot examination include?
cards.a:
• Toe **flexion and extension**
• Ankle **dorsiflexion and plantarflexion**
• Subtalar **inversion and eversion**
• **Ankle jerk (S1-S2)** - often absent in neuropathy
• Note: slide says 'inversion & inversion'; correct is inversion & eversion

cards.q: What does the Wagner classification assess, and what are grades 0 and 1?
cards.a:
• Assesses **ulcer depth** plus presence of **gangrene / loss of perfusion**
• **Grade 0**: intact skin, pre-ulcerative lesion (callus, deformity, healed ulcer)
• **Grade 1**: **superficial ulcer** (skin/subcutis only)
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Wagner climbs from skin -> depth -> abscess/bone -> gangrene.

cards.q: Wagner grade 2 vs grade 3 - what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Grade 2**: deep ulcer reaching **tendon, capsule or bone** but **no abscess or osteomyelitis**
• **Grade 3**: deep ulcer **with abscess, osteomyelitis or joint sepsis**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: 2 = deep but clean; 3 = deep and dirty (pus/bone infection).

cards.q: Wagner grade 4 vs grade 5 - what is the difference?
cards.a:
• **Grade 4**: **localised gangrene** - toes or forefoot
• **Grade 5**: gangrene of the **whole foot**
• Grade 5 usually needs major (below/above-knee) amputation
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: 4 = part of the foot is dead; 5 = the foot is dead.

cards.q: What are the GRADES (depth) of the University of Texas (UT) classification?
cards.a:
• **Grade 0**: pre- or post-ulcerative lesion, completely epithelialised
• **Grade 1**: **superficial** wound, not involving tendon, capsule or bone
• **Grade 2**: penetrates to **tendon or capsule**
• **Grade 3**: penetrates to **bone or joint**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: UT depth 0-3 = skin, superficial, tendon/capsule, bone.

cards.q: What are the STAGES of the UT classification and why is it better than Wagner?
cards.a:
• **A**: clean, non-infected, non-ischaemic
• **B**: **infected**
• **C**: **ischaemic**
• **D**: **infected AND ischaemic**
• Adds infection and ischaemia to depth -> **better predicts amputation** and healing
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: B = Bugs, C = Circulation, D = Double trouble. Risk rises with both grade and stage.

cards.q: Which BEDSIDE investigations are done in a diabetic foot ulcer?
cards.a:
• **Capillary refill time** (> 2 s = poor circulation)
• **Dextrostix** (capillary glucose) - hyper/hypoglycaemia
• **Pedal pulses** (PT, DP) - screen for PAD
• **Ankle-brachial systolic pressure index (ABSI)** - severity of PAD
• **Toe pressure or TcPO2** - local tissue perfusion

cards.q: How is the ankle-brachial systolic pressure index (ABSI) interpreted?
cards.a:
• **< 0.9**: peripheral arterial disease
• **0.9-1.3**: normal
• **> 1.3**: **non-compressible, calcified** vessels - unreliable
• Note: gangrene slide quotes ABI < 1.0; use the < 0.9 cut-off
cards.m: Below 0.9 blocked; above 1.3 rock-hard pipes.

cards.q: Why may the ABSI be falsely reassuring in a diabetic, and what do you use instead?
cards.a:
• **Medial arterial (Mönckeberg) calcification** makes ankle vessels **non-compressible**
• Ankle pressure falsely high -> ABSI normal or **> 1.3** despite PAD
• Use **toe pressure / toe-brachial index** or **transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2)**
cards.m: Toe arteries are spared from calcification - so measure at the toe.

cards.q: Which LABORATORY investigations are sent for a diabetic foot ulcer, and why?
cards.a:
• **HbA1c** - long-term glycaemic control
• **FBS/RBS** - current glucose
• **Deep tissue culture** (if infected) - targeted antibiotics
• **Blood culture** - if sepsis suspected
• **FBC** - anaemia (impairs healing), leucocytosis
• **Renal profile** - AKI, drug dosing

cards.q: Why should a deep tissue sample, not a superficial swab, be sent for culture in an infected DFU?
cards.a:
• Superficial swabs grow **skin colonisers** and miss deep pathogens
• **Deep tissue (or bone) taken after cleansing/debridement** identifies the true causative organism
• Guides **targeted** antibiotic therapy
cards.m: Swab the surface, you culture the passengers; biopsy the depth, you culture the driver.

cards.q: What X-ray findings may be seen in a diabetic foot?
cards.a:
• **Osteolysis** (osteomyelitis)
• **Arterial calcification**
• **Gas shadow** in soft tissue (gas-forming infection)
• **Malalignment** and **peri-articular fragmentation** (Charcot)
• Lecturer pearl: bone changes lag **10-14 days** behind infection

cards.q: What is the role of MRI vs CT in the diabetic foot?
cards.a:
• **MRI**: most sensitive for **osteomyelitis** and **deep abscess** - imaging of choice
• **CT**: assesses **chronic osteomyelitis** - sequestrum, involucrum, cloaca
cards.m: MRI = Marrow and pus; CT = Cortical bits (sequestrum).

cards.q: What is the probe-to-bone test?
cards.a:
• Sterile **blunt metal probe** inserted into the ulcer base
• **Hard, gritty bone felt = positive**
• Positive test strongly suggests **osteomyelitis** -> confirm with X-ray/MRI ± bone biopsy
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: if you can touch bone, assume the bone is infected.

cards.q: What are the four arms of PREVENTIVE management of the diabetic foot?
cards.a:
• **Patient education** - daily foot care; neuropathic patients ignore injury
• **Metabolic control** - individualised glycaemic targets
• **Preventive footwear** - matched to foot risk
• **Preventive surgery** - for deformity causing ulcer/re-ulceration
cards.m: E-M-F-S: Educate, Metabolic, Footwear, Surgery.

cards.q: What footwear advice is given to diabetic patients?
cards.a:
• **Large toe box**, properly **cushioned**
• **Breathable**, appropriate material
• Check inside shoes for **foreign / penetrating bodies** before wearing
• **No thong slippers**; never walk barefoot

cards.q: Name the preventive surgeries for diabetic foot deformity and their purpose.
cards.a:
• **Gastrocnemius-soleus fascia recession** and **Achilles tendon lengthening** - correct equinus, unload forefoot
• **Percutaneous (flexor) tenotomy** - claw/hammer toe tip ulcers
• **Osteotomy** (distal metatarsal) - lets the metatarsal head float up, offloads plantar ulcer
• Aim: prevent ulceration or re-ulceration
cards.m: Tight calf = forefoot hammered with every step - release the calf, rescue the forefoot.

cards.q: What are the adverse effects of gastrocnemius-soleus recession?
cards.a:
• **Subcutaneous haematoma** - resolves within ~3 weeks
• **Sural nerve neurapraxia** - may persist for months
• Benefit: dorsiflexion gain (~14.5°) and high ulcer healing rate
cards.m: Sural nerve runs with the short saphenous vein beside the calf - at risk in calf surgery.

cards.q: How is pain managed in a diabetic foot patient, including neuropathic pain?
cards.a:
• **WHO analgesic ladder**: paracetamol/NSAID -> tramadol -> morphine
• Neuropathic pain adjuvants: **amitriptyline** (TCA), **duloxetine** (SNRI), gabapentinoids
• Caution with NSAIDs in nephropathy
• Note: slide labels duloxetine an anticonvulsant; it is an SNRI antidepressant

cards.q: What are the principles of antimicrobial use in an infected diabetic foot ulcer?
cards.a:
• **Mild** infection: narrow agent, usually **not > 14 days**
• **Moderate/severe**: **broad-spectrum empirical** therapy until **C&S** results, then de-escalate
• Antibiotics are an **adjunct to surgical debridement**, not a substitute
• Topical: mupirocin/bacitracin (Gram +), neomycin/silver sulphadiazine (Gram -); antiseptics iodine, chlorhexidine

cards.q: What are the goals of DFU dressings and which advanced dressings are available?
cards.a:
• Goal: **maintain moisture** and **remove dead tissue**
• Basic: **gauze ± paraffin**
• Advanced: **hydrogel, alginate, hydrofibre, foam, hydrocolloid, hyaluronic acid**
• Lecturer pearl: hydrogel adds moisture to dry slough; alginate/hydrofibre absorb heavy exudate
cards.m: Wet wound -> dry it (alginate); dry wound -> wet it (hydrogel).

cards.q: What are the adjuvant therapies for diabetic foot wounds?
cards.a:
• **Maggot debridement therapy (MDT)** - larvae digest necrotic tissue only
• **Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT)**
• **Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT)** - removes exudate, promotes granulation
cards.m: M-H-N: Maggots, Hyperbaric, Negative pressure.

cards.q: What are the surgical options in DFU management and their indications?
cards.a:
• **Revascularisation** - offer to diabetics with PAD; **antiplatelet** therapy afterwards
• **Surgical debridement** - when non-surgical debridement **fails** OR wound is **deep and infected**
• **Reconstruction** - when primary closure not feasible or secondary healing unreliable

cards.q: What is the key principle of ulcer rehabilitation and which offloading devices are used?
cards.a:
• **Offloading is the key**
• Non-removable: **total contact cast (TCC)** - gold standard for plantar neuropathic ulcers (forced adherence)
• Removable: **removable cast walker**
• Note: slide spells it 'Tocal contact cast'
• Lecturer pearl: avoid TCC in active infection or significant ischaemia
cards.m: A removable device is removed at home - the TCC cannot cheat.

cards.q: Define Charcot neuroarthropathy.
cards.a:
• **Chronic, progressive** destruction of **foot and ankle joints and bones**
• Results from **loss of protective sensation** (neuropathy)
• Diabetes is the commonest cause today
cards.m: A joint that feels nothing gets destroyed by everything.

cards.q: Explain the NEUROTRAUMATIC theory of Charcot neuroarthropathy.
cards.a:
• Sensory neuropathy -> loss of protective pain sensation
• Patient keeps walking on injured bone - **repetitive microtrauma** is painless and unnoticed
• Progressive destruction of bones and joints
cards.m: Like driving on a flat tyre because the dashboard warning light is broken.

cards.q: Explain the NEUROVASCULAR theory of Charcot neuroarthropathy.
cards.a:
• **Autonomic neuropathy** -> persistent vasodilatation -> **increased bone blood flow**
• Mismatch: **osteoclastic resorption > osteoblastic formation**
• **Osteopenia** -> bone weak, fractures and collapses
cards.m: Too much blood washes bone away (hyperaemic osteopenia).

cards.q: What are the clinical features of ACUTE vs CHRONIC Charcot foot?
cards.a:
• **Acute**: **swelling, warmth, erythema**; often little pain; skin temp > 2 °C higher than other foot
• **Chronic**: **rocker-bottom** deformity, **collapse of medial arch**, **bony prominences** -> plantar ulcers
cards.m: Acute = hot red foot; Chronic = flat-bottomed boat (rocker-bottom).

cards.q: How do you clinically distinguish acute Charcot foot from cellulitis?
cards.a:
• **Elevation test**: elevate the leg ~10 min - Charcot redness **settles**, cellulitis redness **persists**
• Charcot: usually **no skin break**, mostly painless, systemically well
• Cellulitis: portal of entry, fever, raised markers
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Charcot blushes and fades when lifted; cellulitis stays angry.

cards.q: Describe the Eichenholtz classification of Charcot neuroarthropathy.
cards.a:
• **Stage 0 (prodromal)**: warm, swollen; X-ray normal, MRI bone oedema
• **Stage I (fragmentation/development)**: fragmentation, subluxation, debris
• **Stage II (coalescence)**: debris absorbed, swelling and warmth reduce
• **Stage III (reconstruction/consolidation)**: bony remodelling, stable deformity
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Prodrome -> Fragment -> Coalesce -> Consolidate (break, glue, set).

cards.q: Describe the Brodsky anatomical classification of Charcot foot.
cards.a:
• **Type 1**: **midfoot** - tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform; **most common**, rocker-bottom
• **Type 2**: **hindfoot** - Chopart and subtalar joints
• **Type 3A**: **ankle** joint
• **Type 3B**: **calcaneal tuberosity** fracture
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: 1 = middle (most), 2 = back, 3 = ankle (A) or heel bone (B).

cards.q: Which bone scan distinguishes Charcot foot from superimposed osteomyelitis?
cards.a:
• **Technetium bone scan**: **positive in both** - cannot differentiate
• **Indium-labelled WBC scan**: **cold (negative)** in neuropathic joint, **hot (positive)** in osteomyelitis
• MRI also struggles to separate infection from Charcot
cards.m: Indium Identifies Infection.

cards.q: Which investigations are done for suspected Charcot neuroarthropathy?
cards.a:
• Labs: **FBC, ESR, CRP** (mainly to look for infection)
• **Plain radiographs**: AP and lateral foot and ankle (weight-bearing if possible)
• **MRI**: early bone marrow oedema, abscess vs soft tissue swelling
• **Bone scan**: superimposed osteomyelitis

cards.q: What is the stage-wise treatment of Charcot neuroarthropathy?
cards.a:
• **Stage 0**: serial X-rays, limited weight bearing, ± pharmacological
• **Stage I**: **total contact casting** with serial review until warmth, swelling and erythema resolve
• **Stage II**: TCC, then **Charcot restraint orthotic walker (CROW)**
• **Stage III**: plantigrade -> **custom inlay shoes**; non-plantigrade/ulcer -> debridement, exostectomy, correction/fusion
cards.m: Hot foot = cast it; cold stable foot = shoe it; ugly ulcerating foot = operate.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment of ACUTE Charcot foot, and what should be avoided?
cards.a:
• **Offloading in a total contact cast** (non-weight bearing initially), until warmth and swelling settle
• Monitor with serial X-rays and skin temperature
• **Antibiotics are NOT indicated** - it is not an infection
• Avoid early surgery on the hot, fragmenting foot
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: treat the hot Charcot foot with a cast, not with cloxacillin.

cards.q: What are the non-operative and operative options for Charcot neuroarthropathy?
cards.a:
• Non-operative: **total contact casting**, **CROW**, **shoewear modification**, **bisphosphonates**
• Operative: **exostectomy** (resect bony prominence) ± **TAL**
• **Deformity correction arthrodesis** ± osteotomies
• **Amputation** for unsalvageable or infected feet

cards.q: What is folliculitis - organisms and typical sites?
cards.a:
• **Superficial inflammation of the hair follicle**
• Commonest organism **Staphylococcus aureus**; also viral (HSV), fungal, parasitic
• Sites: axilla, scalp, face, upper trunk, buttock, groin, legs
• Small, erythematous, **pruritic papules with pustules**
cards.m: One follicle, one pimple.

cards.q: How is folliculitis managed?
cards.a:
• Usually **self-limiting**; good hygiene
• **Topical fusidic acid 2%** or **mupirocin 2%**
• Deep/extensive: **oral cloxacillin 500 mg QID** (6-hourly)
• Refer to dermatologist if recurrent
• Note: slide writes 'QOD' (every other day); correct is QID

cards.q: What is a furuncle (boil) and where does it occur?
cards.a:
• **Collection of pus in the dermis or deeper** around a hair follicle
• Usually follows **folliculitis**
• Sweat and friction sites: **axilla, neck, buttocks**
• Tender erythematous nodule with pustule and spontaneous drainage
cards.m: Folliculitis that went deeper and formed a pus pocket.

cards.q: How is a furuncle managed?
cards.a:
• **Moist heat / warm compresses** - promote localisation and drainage
• Good hygiene
• **Oral cloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5-7 days**
• **Incision and drainage** if fluctuant
• Note: slide says '5oomg QOD'; correct is 500 mg QID

cards.q: What is a carbuncle and how is it treated?
cards.a:
• **Multiple interconnected furuncles** extending into **subcutaneous tissue**, pus from several tracts
• Risk factor: **diabetes**; organism **S. aureus**; sites nape of neck, back, thigh
• Treatment: **incision and drainage (saucerisation)** + **IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID**
cards.m: Carbuncle = a Crowd of boils sharing tunnels.

cards.q: Folliculitis vs furuncle vs carbuncle - what is the key distinction?
cards.a:
• **Folliculitis**: superficial, follicle only -> topical antibiotics
• **Furuncle**: single deeper abscess of a follicle -> warm compress ± oral cloxacillin ± I&D
• **Carbuncle**: several furuncles joined in subcutis, multiple sinuses -> I&D + IV cloxacillin
cards.m: Pimple -> boil -> honeycomb; treatment escalates with depth.

cards.q: What is erysipelas - layer, organism, risk factors and sites?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **superficial dermis** with **superficial lymphatics**
• Organism: **Streptococcus pyogenes** (group A strep)
• Risk factors: previous erysipelas, skin breaks, DM, immunocompromise
• Sites: **lower limbs, face**

cards.q: What does erysipelas look like and how is it treated (Malaysian NAG)?
cards.a:
• **Shiny, tender, erythematous, raised, plaque-like, sharply demarcated** edge
• Cold packs + analgesia
• **Oral penicillin V 500 mg QID**
• Severe: **IV cefuroxime 750 mg TDS**
cards.m: Erysipelas has an Edge you can feel with a fingertip.

cards.q: Erysipelas vs cellulitis - how do you differentiate them?
cards.a:
• **Erysipelas**: superficial dermis + lymphatics; **raised, sharply demarcated** edge; mainly **Strep pyogenes**
• **Cellulitis**: deep dermis + subcutaneous fat; **flat, ill-defined** margin; **S. aureus** and Strep pyogenes
cards.m: Erysipelas = Elevated Edge; Cellulitis = Cloudy margin.

cards.q: What is cellulitis - layer, organisms and risk factors?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue**
• Organisms: **Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes**
• Risk factors: **DM, trauma** (laceration, abrasion), **burns**
• Warm, erythematous, tender, swollen skin

cards.q: How is cellulitis graded by severity (Malaysian NAG)?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: no systemic signs
• **Moderate**: systemic signs (fever, tachycardia) **without hypotension**
• **Severe**: systemic signs **with hypotension**
cards.m: Look at the patient, not the leg: well / septic / shocked.

cards.q: What are the empirical antibiotics for cellulitis by severity (Malaysian NAG)?
cards.a:
• **Mild**: **oral cloxacillin 500 mg QID**
• **Moderate**: **IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID** (6-hourly)
• **Severe**: **IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) 4.5 g** 6-8 hourly
• Note: slide writes 'QOD' for mild; correct is QID
cards.m: Cloxacillin by mouth -> cloxacillin by vein -> Tazocin for shock.

cards.q: What is necrotising fasciitis and what are its risk factors?
cards.a:
• **Life-threatening** bacterial infection spreading **rapidly along fascial planes**
• Risk factors: **immunosuppression (DM, obesity)**, bacterial introduction (**IV drug use, skin abrasions**)
• May or may not be associated with overlying cellulitis

cards.q: What are the EARLY signs of necrotising fasciitis?
cards.a:
• **Pain out of proportion** to clinical findings - severe, constant
• Local erythema or **tense, shiny swelling**
• Fever, malaise, flu-like symptoms
• Tenderness beyond the visible erythema
cards.m: The skin looks innocent but the patient is screaming - think NF.

cards.q: What are the LATE signs of necrotising fasciitis?
cards.a:
• Tense oedema with a **woody feel**
• **Bullae**, **dusky blue/purple** discolouration, skin necrosis
• **Crepitus / surgical emphysema**
• **Septic shock** and multi-organ dysfunction (confusion, anuria)
• Anaesthesia of the skin (nerves destroyed)

cards.q: Describe the microbiological classification (types 1-4) of necrotising fasciitis.
cards.a:
• **Type 1 - polymicrobial** (80-90%): aerobes + anaerobes; diabetics, cancer, post-op abdomen/perineum
• **Type 2 - monomicrobial group A beta-haemolytic strep**: healthy people, limbs (~5%)
• **Type 3 - Vibrio vulnificus**: marine exposure
• **Type 4 - fungal**
cards.m: 1 = Many bugs, 2 = Strep, 3 = Sea, 4 = Spores (fungi).

cards.q: What is the LRINEC score?
cards.a:
• Laboratory Risk Indicator for NEcrotising fasCiitis
• **CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose**
• Score **≥ 6** suspicious; ≥ 8 strongly predictive
• Supports, but **never excludes**, clinical suspicion
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: 'C-W-H-S-C-G' - Can We Help Septic Crumbling Gams?

cards.q: How is necrotising fasciitis diagnosed, and should you wait for imaging?
cards.a:
• **Clinical diagnosis**; confirmed by **surgical exploration and tissue biopsy**
• **Finger test**: grey, dishwater fluid; fascia separates with no resistance; no bleeding
• **Do NOT delay surgery for CT/MRI**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: the operating theatre is the investigation of choice.

cards.q: What is the management of necrotising fasciitis?
cards.a:
• **Emergent radical debridement** of all necrotic tissue, with planned re-look in ~24 h
• **Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics** (penicillin, clindamycin, metronidazole, aminoglycoside), then culture-directed
• Resuscitation/ICU
• **Low threshold for amputation** when life-threatening
cards.m: Cut early, cut wide, cut again.

cards.q: Why is clindamycin included in the antibiotic regimen for necrotising fasciitis?
cards.a:
• Inhibits **bacterial protein synthesis** -> **suppresses toxin production** (streptococcal/clostridial exotoxins)
• Works regardless of bacterial growth phase (penicillin fails at high bacterial load - Eagle effect)
• Always combined with penicillin/broad-spectrum cover
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: penicillin kills the bugs; clindamycin switches off their toxin factory.

cards.q: Define gangrene and name its three types.
cards.a:
• **Tissue death** due to **infection, ischaemia or both**
• **Dry** - ischaemia without infection
• **Wet** - ischaemic tissue becomes infected
• **Gas** - Clostridium infection with gas in tissues

cards.q: What causes dry gangrene and what does it look like?
cards.a:
• **Prolonged ischaemia without infection** - atherosclerosis narrowing peripheral arteries
• Risk factors: DM, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia
• **Black, dry, shrunken, mummified** tissue with a clear line of demarcation
cards.m: Dry gangrene = mummy: dry, black and stable.

cards.q: What is wet gangrene and why is it common in diabetics?
cards.a:
• **Ischaemic tissue that becomes infected**
• Diabetics: impaired wound healing, immunopathy, neuropathy
• Swollen, moist, foul-smelling, spreading - a **surgical emergency** (sepsis risk)
cards.m: Wet = infected = urgent; dry = stable = revascularise.

cards.q: What causes gas gangrene and what are its features?
cards.a:
• **Clostridium species** (mainly **C. perfringens**) - contaminated traumatic or surgical wounds; spontaneous in immunocompromised
• **Severe pain**, swelling, discolouration, **crepitus**, haemorrhagic blisters
• **Rapid progression**, gas on X-ray, **high mortality**
cards.m: Gas gangrene crackles - Clostridium makes bubbles.

cards.q: Which investigations are done for gangrene?
cards.a:
• **FBC** (WCC, inflammatory markers), **HbA1c**
• **ABI** - **< 0.9** = arterial insufficiency (unreliable if > 1.3 calcified)
• **X-ray** - gas in tissues; **CT/MRI** - depth and extent
• **Wound cultures and Gram stain**
• Note: slide gives ABI < 1.0; the accepted PAD cut-off is < 0.9

cards.q: How is each type of gangrene treated, and what is the prognosis?
cards.a:
• **Dry**: restore blood flow - **antiplatelet, statin, BP control** + **revascularisation** (endovascular/surgical)
• **Wet or gas**: **urgent surgical debridement / amputation** + **broad-spectrum antibiotics**
• Prognosis: DM + critical limb ischaemia - up to **50% amputation or death within 1 year**; gas gangrene high mortality

cards.q: What is a felon and where does it occur?
cards.a:
• **Subcutaneous abscess of the fingertip pulp**
• **15-20%** of hand infections
• Most common in the **thumb and index finger**
• Clinical diagnosis; **no history of injury in 50%**
cards.m: Felon = Fingertip pulp abscess.

cards.q: What are the causes and organisms of a felon?
cards.a:
• Penetrating injury: **glucose-monitoring needlestick**, splinters; spread from paronychia
• **Staphylococcus aureus** - most common
• Gram-negatives - immunosuppressed
• **Eikenella corrodens** - diabetics who **bite their nails**
cards.m: The glucometer lancet is the diabetic's felon gun.

cards.q: What is the key examination finding of a felon and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• Severe **throbbing pain**, tense tender pulp
• Swelling **does NOT extend proximal to the DIP flexion crease**
• Swelling beyond it suggests **flexor sheath or joint** involvement
• Pulp septa create closed compartments -> complications: **fingertip compartment syndrome, flexor tenosynovitis, osteomyelitis, digital tip necrosis**
cards.m: The DIP crease is the felon's fence.

cards.q: How is a felon treated and when is an X-ray needed?
cards.a:
• **Early felon (no drainable abscess)**: oral antibiotics + observation
• **Abscess**: **bedside I&D + IV antibiotics** - lateral (midaxial) incision avoiding the pulp tactile surface and digital neurovascular bundle; avoid fish-mouth incisions
• **X-ray only if trauma** - exclude fracture/foreign body

cards.q: Herpetic whitlow vs felon - how do you tell them apart and why does it matter?
cards.a:
• **Herpetic whitlow** (HSV): **clear vesicles**, burning pain, pulp **not tense**; often healthcare/dental workers or children
• **Felon**: tense, throbbing pulp with pus
• Whitlow: **do NOT incise** (spreads infection, bacterial superinfection) - give **acyclovir**, it is self-limiting
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: vesicles = virus = no knife.

cards.q: What is pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis - risk factors and organisms?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **synovial sheath around a flexor tendon**
• 2.5-9.4% of hand infections
• Risk factors: **DM, IVDU, immunocompromise**
• Mechanism: penetrating trauma; spread from felon, septic joint, deep space
• Organisms: **S. aureus** (most common), S. epidermidis, Pseudomonas

cards.q: What are the four Kanavel signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis?
cards.a:
• **Flexed posture** of the digit
• **Tenderness along the tendon sheath**
• **Pain on passive extension**
• **Fusiform (sausage) swelling** of the digit
cards.m: FFTP: Flexed, Fusiform, Tender sheath, Passive-stretch pain.

cards.q: Which Kanavel sign is the most specific and usually the earliest?
cards.a:
• **Pain on passive extension** of the digit
• Stretching the inflamed, pus-filled sheath causes exquisite pain
• Fusiform swelling is the commonest sign
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Passive extension = Pus in the sheath.

cards.q: How is pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis managed?
cards.a:
• **Non-operative (rare)**: early presentation only - admit, **IV antibiotics, splint/immobilise, elevate**, review within **24 h**
• **Operative**: **I&D / irrigation of the flexor sheath** + culture-specific IV antibiotics
• Operate if **late presentation**, **no improvement in 24 h**; low threshold
cards.m: Give antibiotics 24 hours to prove themselves - then knife.

cards.q: What are the complications of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis?
cards.a:
• **Stiffness** (adhesions)
• **Tendon / pulley rupture** or necrosis
• **Loss of soft tissue**
• **Osteomyelitis**
• **Spread of infection** (deep spaces, horseshoe abscess)

cards.q: Which deep fascial spaces of the hand get infected and how does each present?
cards.a:
• Entry: puncture, bite, crush
• **Thenar space**: pain on **thumb flexion**, thumb held abducted, first web swelling
• **Hypothenar**: pain on **little finger flexion**
• **Midpalmar**: pain on **middle, ring and little finger flexion**, loss of palmar concavity
• All: **dorsal hand swelling** (lax dorsal skin and lymphatics)

cards.q: How are deep fascial space infections of the hand investigated and treated?
cards.a:
• **Plain X-ray** AP and lateral (foreign body, gas, bone)
• **MRI** for extent
• Treatment: **incision and drainage** followed by **IV antibiotics**
cards.m: Pus in a closed space must be let out - antibiotics alone fail.

cards.q: Acute vs chronic paronychia - what is the difference?
cards.a:
• Infection of the **proximal/lateral nail folds**; cuticle barrier disrupted
• **Acute (< 6 weeks)**: bacterial (**S. aureus**) - pain, redness, swelling, **pus at nail fold**
• **Chronic (> 6 weeks)**: often fungal (**Candida albicans**) or mixed - nail fold thickening, mild pain; wet-work occupations
cards.m: Acute = Aureus; Chronic = Candida.

cards.q: How is paronychia treated?
cards.a:
• **No abscess**: warm soaks **5-6 times/day for 10-15 min** + triple antibiotic ointment
• **Abscess**: **incision and drainage** (elevate the nail fold)
• **Chronic**: avoid trauma and wet work; **topical/systemic antifungals** (itraconazole, terbinafine)
• Differentials: felon, herpetic whitlow, onychomycosis, psoriasis, SCC

cards.q: What is a horseshoe abscess and how does it spread?
cards.a:
• Infection spreading between the **radial bursa** (FPL/thumb sheath) and **ulnar bursa** (little finger sheath)
• Bursae communicate via **Parona's space** (distal forearm, deep to FDP, superficial to pronator quadratus)
• Swollen, red, shiny **thumb AND little finger** with palm pain
• Note: slide places Parona's space in the mid-palm; it lies in the distal forearm
cards.m: Thumb and little finger joined by a U-shaped tunnel = horseshoe.

cards.q: How is a horseshoe abscess investigated and treated, and what are its complications?
cards.a:
• Investigate: **FBC, CRP, ESR**; **X-ray, MRI**
• Treat: **IV antibiotics + incision and drainage** (Brunner incisions), then **regular physiotherapy**
• Complications: **hand stiffness and loss of function**, **tendon necrosis/rupture**

cards.q: What are the two mechanisms of human bite injury?
cards.a:
• **Occlusal (direct) bite**: tissue crushed between upper and lower teeth
• **Clenched-fist injury (fight bite)**: knuckle strikes teeth - usually **3rd/4th MCP joints**; bacteria driven into **tendon, joint or bone**

cards.q: Why is a small 'fight bite' laceration over the knuckle so dangerous, and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• Wound made with fist **clenched**; when fingers extend, the tendon/capsule wound **slides away** and seals contamination inside the MCP joint
• Risk of **septic arthritis, tenosynovitis, osteomyelitis**
• **X-ray**, **surgical exploration and washout**, leave open, **amoxicillin-clavulanate**
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: any laceration over a knuckle is a human bite until proven otherwise.

cards.q: What organisms cause human bite infections and what is the prophylaxis?
cards.a:
• **Eikenella corrodens**, **Staphylococcus aureus**, **viridans streptococci**, anaerobes
• Irrigate thoroughly with saline or sterile water
• All bites that pierce skin: **amoxicillin-clavulanate for ~1 week**
• Note: slide spells 'Eikonella'; correct is Eikenella
cards.m: Lecturer pearl: Eikenella resists cloxacillin and clindamycin - co-amoxiclav covers it.

cards.q: Dog bite vs cat bite - how do the wounds differ and which is more likely to get infected?
cards.a:
• **Dog**: crush, puncture, avulsion, tears, abrasions (big blunt jaw)
• **Cat**: small sharp teeth -> **deep puncture wounds that seal immediately**
• **Cat bites have the higher infection risk** (bacteria inoculated deep, e.g. into tendon sheath or joint)
cards.m: Dogs tear, cats inject.

cards.q: What is the commonest organism in cat and dog bite infections?
cards.a:
• **Pasteurella species** (P. multocida) - most common in both
• Most infections **polymicrobial**, with at least one anaerobe
• Pasteurella infections appear quickly (within 12-24 h)
cards.m: Pets carry Pasteurella.

cards.q: How are cat and dog bites managed?
cards.a:
• **Copious irrigation**
• **Prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate**
• **Tetanus toxoid**; **± rabies prophylaxis** if any suspicion about the animal's behaviour
• **Formal surgical debridement** if crush injury, foreign bodies or abscess

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 15 years has a plantar ulcer under the first metatarsal head. After debridement a sterile probe reaches the flexor tendon and joint capsule but does not touch bone. There is no pus, no surrounding cellulitis, and the X-ray shows no bony erosion. Foot pulses are palpable.
What is the Wagner grade of this ulcer?
mcq.e: Wagner grades depth then complications: grade 1 superficial, grade 2 deep to tendon, capsule or bone but without abscess or osteomyelitis, grade 3 deep with abscess or osteomyelitis, grades 4-5 gangrene. This ulcer is deep (tendon/capsule) but clean, so grade 2. Lecturer pearl: the Wagner table was image-only on the slides.
w: Wrong - grade 1 is confined to skin and subcutis; this reaches tendon and capsule.
Wrong - grade 3 needs abscess, osteomyelitis or joint sepsis, none of which is present.
Correct - deep to tendon/capsule without abscess or osteomyelitis = grade 2.
Wrong - grade 4 means localised gangrene of toes or forefoot.
Wrong - grade 0 is intact skin or a pre-ulcerative lesion.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old woman with diabetes has a foot ulcer over the fifth metatarsal head. The probe touches gritty bone. There is purulent discharge and erythema 3 cm around the wound. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are easily palpable and the ABSI is 1.05.
How is this wound classified using the University of Texas system?
mcq.e: The UT system pairs depth (grade 0-3) with stage: A clean, B infected, C ischaemic, D infected and ischaemic. Probe to bone makes it grade 3; pus and cellulitis with normal pulses and a normal ABSI make it infected but not ischaemic, stage B. Lecturer pearl: because UT adds infection and ischaemia it predicts amputation better than Wagner.
w: Correct - penetrates to bone (grade 3), infected without ischaemia (stage B).
Wrong - grade 2 reaches tendon or capsule only; this probe touches bone.
Wrong - stage D needs ischaemia as well; pulses and ABSI are normal.
Wrong - the probe touches bone (grade 3) and there is no ischaemia for stage D.
Wrong - stage C is ischaemia without infection; this wound is infected and well perfused.

mcq.stem:
A 70-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and nephropathy complains of night pain in the right forefoot. Pedal pulses are impalpable and the toes are cool. Ankle cuff pressures cannot be occluded even at 250 mmHg, giving an ABSI of 1.5. X-ray shows linear calcification of the tibial arteries.
Which test should be used next to assess limb perfusion?
o: Repeat ABSI with a wider cuff
No further test; ABSI above 1.3 excludes PAD
Capillary refill time of the hallux
Plain X-ray of the foot in two views
mcq.e: An ABSI above 1.3 means the ankle vessels are non-compressible from medial arterial calcification, common in diabetics and renal disease, so the reading is falsely high and unreliable. Digital arteries are usually spared, so toe pressure (toe-brachial index) or transcutaneous oxygen pressure gives a true measure of perfusion. ABSI below 0.9 indicates PAD and 0.9-1.3 is normal.
w: Wrong - a bigger cuff cannot compress calcified vessels; the result stays falsely high.
Wrong - a high ABSI is unreliable, not reassuring; symptoms here suggest ischaemia.
Wrong - CRT is a crude bedside screen and does not quantify perfusion.
Correct - toe pressure or TcPO2 bypasses calcified ankle vessels.
Wrong - X-ray has already shown calcification; it does not measure perfusion.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old diabetic has clawing of all lesser toes with prominent metatarsal heads and thick plantar callus beneath them. The fat pad appears displaced distally. Sensation to monofilament is absent at several sites.
Which mechanism best explains the toe deformity?
o: Sensory neuropathy alone causing unnoticed trauma
mcq.e: Motor neuropathy weakens the intrinsic foot muscles so the long flexors and extensors act unopposed, producing claw toes and pulling the protective fat pad forward. The metatarsal heads then carry high plantar pressure, forming callus and later ulcers. Sensory loss explains why the patient does not notice the damage, but not the deformity itself.
w: Wrong - autonomic neuropathy causes dry cracked skin and AV shunting, not clawing.
Correct - intrinsic weakness leads to claw toes and prominent metatarsal heads.
Wrong - digital ischaemia causes pain and gangrene, not a dynamic toe deformity.
Wrong - sensory loss removes the warning of injury but does not deform the toes.
Wrong - immunopathy affects infection spread, not toe posture.

mcq.stem:
A 49-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes attends the primary care clinic for her annual foot screen. She has no wounds. The doctor wants to identify whether she has lost the level of sensation that protects her from unnoticed injury, as recommended in the Malaysian diabetic foot CPG.
Which test is most appropriate?
o: 128 Hz tuning fork over the medial malleolus
Ankle jerk reflex with a tendon hammer
Pinprick with a sterile needle on the dorsum
Two-point discrimination over the toe pulps
mcq.e: Loss of protective sensation is defined by inability to feel a 10 g monofilament pressed until it buckles at standard plantar sites (hallux, metatarsal heads, midfoot, heel, toe pulps). The 128 Hz tuning fork and ankle reflexes add information about large-fibre neuropathy but do not define LOPS. The tuning fork should be applied to a distal bony point such as the hallux, not the malleolus.
w: Wrong - vibration is a supplementary test and is applied distally (hallux), not at the malleolus.
Wrong - an absent ankle jerk supports neuropathy but does not define protective sensation.
Wrong - pinprick is useful for glove-and-stocking loss but is not the standard LOPS test.
Wrong - two-point discrimination is a hand test, not a diabetic foot screen.
Correct - the 10 g monofilament is the standard test for loss of protective sensation.

mcq.stem:
In a diabetic foot clinic, a 60-year-old man asks how likely he is to develop a foot ulcer. He has type 2 diabetes for 8 years and the following history items are recorded.
Which of these is the strongest predictor of a future foot ulcer?
o: A previous ulcer that has healed
mcq.e: Previous ulceration and previous amputation are listed as local risk factors, and a healed ulcer marks a foot that already has the neuropathy, deformity and pressure pattern that caused it, giving a very high recurrence rate. Poor glycaemic control and smoking are systemic risk factors but are weaker predictors. Lecturer pearl: patients in remission from an ulcer are the highest-risk group for intensive follow-up.
w: Wrong - poor glycaemic control is a risk factor but a weaker predictor than previous ulcer.
Correct - a previous ulcer (or amputation) is the strongest predictor of a new ulcer.
Wrong - hypertension is a vascular risk factor, not a strong direct ulcer predictor.
Wrong - obesity is not a listed predictor of foot ulceration.
Wrong - smoking is a systemic risk factor but less predictive than a previous ulcer.

mcq.stem:
A 67-year-old diabetic smoker has a painful, pale, sloughy ulcer at the tip of the second toe. Pain is worse at night and eased by hanging the leg over the bed. The foot is cool, hairless and pulseless, capillary refill is 5 seconds, and monofilament sensation is intact at all sites.
What type of ulcer is this?
mcq.e: Ischaemic ulcers occur at toe tips and foot margins, are painful with a pale sloughy base, and come with a cold, pulseless foot and rest pain relieved by dependency. Neuropathic ulcers are painless, on plantar pressure points with a callus rim, in a warm foot with pulses. Intact sensation here excludes a neuroischaemic picture. Lecturer pearl: this contrast was not spelt out on the slides.
w: Wrong - neuropathic ulcers are painless, plantar, callused, with sensory loss.
Wrong - venous ulcers lie in the gaiter area with oedema and pigmentation.
Wrong - pressure ulcers occur over heels/sacrum in immobile patients.
Correct - toe-tip, painful, cold, pulseless foot with intact sensation = ischaemic.
Wrong - neuroischaemic ulcers need neuropathy too; sensation is intact here.

mcq.stem:
A 72-year-old woman with diabetes presents with black, dry, shrivelled second and third toes with a clear line of demarcation at the metatarsophalangeal level. The rest of the forefoot, midfoot and heel are viable. There is no pus.
What is the Wagner grade?
mcq.e: Wagner grades 4 and 5 are defined by gangrene: grade 4 is localised to toes or forefoot, grade 5 involves the whole foot. Gangrene limited to two toes with a viable remaining foot is grade 4. Grade 3 is a deep ulcer with abscess or osteomyelitis but no gangrene. Lecturer pearl: Wagner table was image-only on the slides.
w: Correct - localised gangrene of toes = grade 4.
Wrong - grade 3 is deep infection (abscess/osteomyelitis) without gangrene.
Wrong - grade 5 is gangrene of the whole foot; here the foot is mostly viable.
Wrong - grade 2 is a deep ulcer without infection or gangrene.
Wrong - grade 1 is a superficial ulcer.

mcq.stem:
A 64-year-old diabetic man has a shallow 1 cm ulcer on the dorsum of the hallux that does not reach tendon. The base is clean with no discharge or erythema. Foot pulses are absent and his ABSI is 0.6.
How is this wound classified using the University of Texas system?
mcq.e: A superficial wound not reaching tendon, capsule or bone is UT grade 1. Absent pulses with an ABSI below 0.9 indicate ischaemia, and the absence of discharge or erythema means no infection, so stage C. Stage D would require infection as well as ischaemia.
w: Wrong - stage A is non-ischaemic; ABSI 0.6 indicates PAD.
Wrong - stage B is infected; there are no signs of infection.
Wrong - grade 2 reaches tendon or capsule; this ulcer is superficial.
Wrong - stage D requires infection plus ischaemia.
Correct - superficial (grade 1) and ischaemic without infection (stage C).

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has deep painful fissures over both heels. The feet are warm and dry with no sweating, the dorsal veins are distended, and the pedal pulses are bounding.
Which component of diabetic neuropathy best explains these findings?
mcq.e: Autonomic neuropathy abolishes sweating, leaving dry skin that cracks and fissures and lets bacteria in. It also opens arteriovenous shunts, giving a warm foot with distended veins and bounding pulses despite poor nutritive flow. The same increased bone blood flow underlies the neurovascular theory of Charcot foot.
w: Wrong - sensory loss removes pain warnings but does not cause dry skin or shunting.
Wrong - motor neuropathy causes claw toes and pressure points.
Correct - anhidrosis and AV shunting are autonomic effects.
Wrong - macrovascular PAD causes a cold, pulseless foot.
Wrong - immunopathy impairs infection control, not sweating or vessel tone.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old woman with diabetes has a 3-week-old plantar ulcer under the second metatarsal head. A sterile probe touches hard, gritty bone. She is afebrile, CRP is 48 mg/L, and plain X-rays taken today are normal.
Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm or exclude osteomyelitis?
mcq.e: A positive probe-to-bone test strongly suggests osteomyelitis, and plain X-ray changes lag 10-14 days behind infection, so a normal film does not exclude it. MRI is the most sensitive test for osteomyelitis and deep abscess in the diabetic foot. CT is better reserved for chronic osteomyelitis (sequestrum, involucrum, cloaca), and technetium scans are non-specific.
w: Correct - MRI is the most sensitive investigation for osteomyelitis and deep abscess.
Wrong - CT shows chronic changes such as sequestrum but is less sensitive early.
Wrong - waiting months delays treatment of likely osteomyelitis.
Wrong - technetium scans are positive in many non-infective conditions, including Charcot.
Wrong - ultrasound cannot assess bone marrow.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old man with diabetes has an infected heel ulcer with purulent discharge and 3 cm of surrounding erythema. He is to start empirical antibiotics and the team wants a sample that identifies the true causative organism.
Which specimen is most appropriate?
o: Swab of the surrounding intact skin
Swab of exudate on the old dressing
mcq.e: Superficial swabs of a chronic ulcer grow colonising skin flora and can mislead antibiotic choice. Deep tissue (or bone) taken after cleansing and debridement represents the infecting organism and allows targeted therapy once C&S results return. Blood cultures are added if sepsis is suspected.
w: Wrong - superficial swabs culture colonisers rather than the pathogen.
Wrong - intact skin flora is irrelevant to the deep infection.
Correct - deep tissue after debridement identifies the causative organism.
Wrong - urine culture does not help a foot infection.
Wrong - old dressing exudate is heavily contaminated.

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old man with diabetic neuropathy has a 2 cm clean plantar ulcer under the first metatarsal head that has not healed in 3 months despite dressings. There is no infection, pedal pulses are palpable and the ABSI is 1.0. He admits removing his prescribed boot at home.
What is the most effective offloading method?
mcq.e: Offloading is the key to healing a plantar neuropathic ulcer. A non-removable total contact cast is the gold standard because it redistributes plantar pressure and cannot be taken off, guaranteeing adherence, which is why it outperforms removable walkers. It is suitable here because there is no infection and no significant ischaemia. Note: slide spells it 'Tocal contact cast'.
w: Wrong - removable walkers fail when patients take them off, as this patient does.
Wrong - strict bed rest is impractical and carries thromboembolic and deconditioning risks.
Wrong - insoles are for prevention, not for healing an active ulcer.
Wrong - neuropathic patients rarely comply with partial weight bearing.
Correct - a non-removable TCC is the gold standard offloading method.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old woman with diabetes has a superficial toe ulcer with 1 cm of surrounding erythema and slight purulence. She is systemically well, with no deep tissue involvement. Pulses are palpable. Oral antibiotics are started together with wound care.
What is the appropriate maximum duration of antibiotics for this infection?
mcq.e: For mild diabetic foot infection, antibiotics should be narrow-spectrum and usually not continued beyond 14 days; prolonged therapy promotes resistance and adverse effects without improving healing. Antibiotics treat infection, not the ulcer itself, so they are not continued until epithelialisation. Six weeks or longer is reserved for osteomyelitis.
w: Wrong - 3 days is too short for a soft tissue diabetic foot infection.
Wrong - 6 weeks is the duration for osteomyelitis, not mild soft tissue infection.
Wrong - antibiotics treat infection, not an uninfected healing wound.
Correct - mild infection: should not exceed 14 days.
Wrong - months of therapy has no role in mild infection.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old diabetic man has a forefoot ulcer with spreading erythema to the ankle, a deep plantar collection, temperature 38.8 °C and heart rate 112/min. Deep tissue samples have been sent and surgical debridement is planned.
What is the most appropriate antibiotic strategy?
o: Oral cloxacillin and review in two weeks
Broad-spectrum IV, then tailor to C&S
Oral metronidazole alone as anaerobic cover
mcq.e: Moderate and severe diabetic foot infections are often polymicrobial and need broad-spectrum empirical therapy started promptly, then narrowed once culture and sensitivity results are available. Antibiotics act as an adjunct to surgical debridement of the collection. Topical agents and narrow oral regimens are inadequate for systemic infection.
w: Wrong - a narrow oral agent is suitable only for mild infection.
Correct - broad-spectrum empirical IV therapy, de-escalated per C&S.
Wrong - topical agents cannot treat deep or systemic infection.
Wrong - delaying antibiotics in a septic patient is dangerous.
Wrong - metronidazole alone misses Gram-positive and aerobic Gram-negative organisms.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old diabetic woman has a 3 cm cavity ulcer on the lateral foot after debridement of an abscess. Infection is controlled, but the wound produces heavy exudate that soaks through gauze twice a day, macerating the surrounding skin.
Which dressing is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Dressings aim to maintain a moist (not wet) environment and remove dead tissue. Alginate (and hydrofibre) dressings absorb large volumes of exudate and can pack cavities, protecting the skin from maceration. Hydrogel donates moisture and suits dry sloughy wounds; hydrocolloids are occlusive and suit low-exudate wounds. Lecturer pearl: dressing choice by exudate was not detailed on the slides.
w: Wrong - hydrogel adds moisture and would worsen maceration.
Wrong - dry gauze is a basic dressing that will saturate and adhere.
Wrong - hydrocolloid is occlusive, for low-exudate wounds.
Correct - alginate absorbs heavy exudate and fills cavities.
Wrong - paraffin gauze is a basic non-adherent contact layer with little absorbency.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with diabetes has had three recurrences of a plantar forefoot ulcer under the metatarsal heads. Ankle dorsiflexion is limited to -5° with the knee extended but improves to 15° when the knee is flexed. The ulcer is currently healed and pulses are normal.
Which preventive procedure is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Equinus increases forefoot plantar pressure and drives recurrent forefoot ulcers. Dorsiflexion that improves with knee flexion (Silfverskiöld test) shows that the tightness is in the gastrocnemius, which crosses the knee, so gastrocnemius-soleus fascia recession is indicated; tightness that persists with the knee flexed would favour Achilles tendon lengthening. Lecturer pearl: the Silfverskiöld test is beyond the slides.
w: Wrong - osteotomy offloads a single metatarsal head but does not correct the equinus.
Correct - isolated gastrocnemius tightness is treated by gastrocnemius recession.
Wrong - amputation is not a preventive procedure for a healed ulcer.
Wrong - flexor tenotomy treats toe-tip ulcers from clawed toes.
Wrong - arthrodesis would stiffen the ankle and worsen forefoot loading.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old woman with diabetic neuropathy has a recurrent ulcer on the tip of the third toe. The toe is held in flexion at the interphalangeal joints but can be passively straightened. Pulses are palpable, the ulcer is clean, and X-ray shows no osteomyelitis.
Which procedure is most appropriate to prevent recurrence?
mcq.e: A flexible claw or hammer toe loads the toe tip, producing apical ulcers. Percutaneous flexor tenotomy releases the deforming tendon, letting the toe straighten; toe-tip ulcers without osteomyelitis heal in about 3 weeks with very few complications. Calf procedures address forefoot pressure from equinus, not toe-tip ulcers.
w: Correct - flexor tenotomy straightens a flexible clawed toe and heals tip ulcers.
Wrong - gastrocnemius recession treats equinus-driven forefoot ulcers.
Wrong - Achilles lengthening also targets equinus, not toe flexion.
Wrong - amputation is excessive for a clean ulcer without osteomyelitis.
Wrong - a TCC offloads the plantar forefoot and does not correct the toe deformity.

mcq.stem:
A 71-year-old diabetic smoker has a 4-month non-healing ulcer on the lateral border of the foot. The foot is cold and pulseless with rest pain, ABSI is 0.45, and there are no signs of infection. Duplex ultrasound shows a short occlusion of the superficial femoral artery.
What is the most appropriate next step?
mcq.e: Revascularisation should be offered to diabetic patients with peripheral arterial disease, as no wound will heal without inflow. A short occlusion is amenable to endovascular or surgical revascularisation, followed by antiplatelet therapy. Total contact casts are avoided in significant ischaemia, and adjuvants such as HBOT or MDT do not replace restoring blood flow.
w: Wrong - TCC is avoided in significant ischaemia and does not fix inflow.
Wrong - HBOT is an adjuvant, not a substitute for revascularisation.
Correct - ischaemic ulcers need revascularisation, then antiplatelet therapy.
Wrong - amputation is premature when the lesion is revascularisable.
Wrong - maggots debride slough but cannot heal an ischaemic wound.

mcq.stem:
A 56-year-old man with diabetic neuropathy has a 2-week history of a swollen, red, warm left midfoot with no skin break. He is afebrile, WCC is 8.9 × 10^9/L, and the foot is 3 °C warmer than the right. The redness fades markedly after 10 minutes of leg elevation. X-rays are normal; MRI shows midfoot bone marrow oedema.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral NSAIDs and full weight bearing
mcq.e: A hot, swollen, painless foot without a portal of entry, a temperature difference above 2 °C, redness that settles on elevation and normal X-rays with MRI marrow oedema indicate acute (Eichenholtz stage 0) Charcot foot, not cellulitis. Treatment is offloading and immobilisation in a total contact cast with serial review. Antibiotics are not indicated and surgery is avoided in the active phase. Lecturer pearl: elevation test and stage 0 are beyond the slides.
w: Wrong - no infection: redness settling on elevation favours Charcot over cellulitis.
Wrong - continued weight bearing drives fragmentation and collapse.
Wrong - there is no necrotic or infected tissue to debride.
Wrong - exostectomy is for chronic stage III prominences, not the acute foot.
Correct - acute Charcot is treated by offloading in a total contact cast.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old woman with long-standing Charcot midfoot deformity develops a plantar ulcer over the collapsed cuboid with rising CRP. MRI shows marrow oedema throughout the midfoot that the radiologist cannot confidently attribute to infection or to the neuropathic joint.
Which investigation best distinguishes superimposed osteomyelitis from Charcot arthropathy?
mcq.e: Technetium bone scans are positive in both neuropathic joints and osteomyelitis, and MRI struggles to separate them. An indium-labelled white cell scan is typically cold in a neuropathic joint and hot in osteomyelitis, so it is used to detect superimposed infection. Bone biopsy remains the definitive test if doubt persists.
w: Wrong - X-ray changes of Charcot and osteomyelitis overlap.
Wrong - technetium uptake is increased in both Charcot and osteomyelitis.
Wrong - CT shows bony architecture but not active infection reliably.
Wrong - MRI is already equivocal; contrast does not resolve this well.
Correct - indium WBC scan is cold in Charcot and hot in osteomyelitis.

mcq.stem:
A 59-year-old diabetic man has a 6-week history of a warm, swollen right foot. The foot remains 3 °C warmer than the left. Weight-bearing X-rays now show bony debris, fragmentation of the tarsometatarsal joints and early subluxation.
Which Eichenholtz stage is this?
mcq.e: Eichenholtz staging follows the radiographic evolution: stage 0 has clinical inflammation with normal X-rays, stage I (fragmentation/development) shows debris, fragmentation and subluxation in a hot foot, stage II (coalescence) shows absorption of debris with reducing warmth, and stage III (reconstruction) shows remodelling and a stable deformity. There is no stage IV. Lecturer pearl: Eichenholtz table was image-only on the slides.
w: Correct - fragmentation and subluxation in a hot foot = stage I.
Wrong - stage 0 has normal X-rays.
Wrong - stage II shows coalescence with absorption of debris and reducing warmth.
Wrong - stage III is a cool, consolidated, remodelled foot.
Wrong - Eichenholtz has no stage IV.

mcq.stem:
A 65-year-old woman with diabetic neuropathy has a cool, painless foot with a rocker-bottom sole and collapse of the medial arch. Lateral X-ray shows dorsal dislocation at the junction of the metatarsal bases and the cuneiforms.
Which joint complex is primarily involved?
mcq.e: Brodsky type 1, involving the tarsometatarsal and naviculocuneiform joints, is the most common pattern of Charcot foot and produces the classic rocker-bottom deformity with medial arch collapse. Type 2 is the hindfoot (Chopart and subtalar), type 3A the ankle and type 3B a calcaneal tuberosity fracture. Lecturer pearl: Brodsky table was image-only on the slides.
w: Wrong - ankle involvement (type 3A) causes instability, not a rocker-bottom midfoot.
Correct - TMT (Lisfranc) involvement, Brodsky type 1, causes rocker-bottom foot.
Wrong - hindfoot (type 2) involvement causes hindfoot instability.
Wrong - calcaneal tuberosity fracture is type 3B.
Wrong - forefoot joints are not part of the Brodsky types and do not cause rocker-bottom.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man with chronic consolidated Charcot foot has a fixed, non-plantigrade midfoot with a bony plantar prominence. He has had recurrent ulcers over this prominence despite custom footwear. The foot is cool and the ulcer is currently healed; there is no osteomyelitis.
What is the most appropriate management?
mcq.e: In Eichenholtz stage III the foot is consolidated. A plantigrade foot can be managed with custom inlay shoes, but a non-plantigrade foot or recurrent ulceration over a bony prominence needs surgery: exostectomy (often with Achilles lengthening) or deformity correction and fusion with internal fixation. Amputation is reserved for unsalvageable feet.
w: Wrong - casting is for the active stages, not a consolidated deformity.
Wrong - footwear alone has already failed in this non-plantigrade foot.
Wrong - bisphosphonates have a possible role in the acute phase only.
Correct - stage III with recurrent ulcer over a prominence: exostectomy.
Wrong - the foot is salvageable, so amputation is not first-line.

mcq.stem:
A 54-year-old woman with diabetic autonomic neuropathy develops a Charcot ankle. She asks why her bones became so weak. DEXA of the affected foot shows marked regional osteopenia compared with the other side.
Which mechanism best explains this osteopenia?
mcq.e: The neurovascular theory proposes that autonomic neuropathy causes persistent vasodilatation and increased bone blood flow, so osteoclastic resorption exceeds osteoblastic formation, producing osteopenia that fractures under load. The neurotraumatic theory adds repeated unnoticed microtrauma from loss of protective sensation. Infection, gout and ischaemia are not the mechanism.
w: Wrong - Charcot bone has increased, not reduced, blood flow.
Wrong - Charcot is non-infective.
Correct - autonomic hyperaemia shifts the balance towards osteoclastic resorption.
Wrong - gout is a crystal arthropathy unrelated to Charcot.
Wrong - she has kept walking; disuse is not the driver of Charcot osteopenia.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old woman with diabetes presents with a 1-day history of fever and a painful red area on her left cheek. There is a bright red, shiny, raised plaque with a sharply demarcated edge that can be felt with a fingertip. There is no fluctuance and no pustule.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics, so lymphatic oedema produces a raised plaque with a sharp, palpable margin; it is caused mainly by Streptococcus pyogenes and favours the face and lower limbs. Cellulitis lies deeper (deep dermis and subcutis) and has a flat, ill-defined edge. Necrotising fasciitis is suggested by pain out of proportion, bullae and systemic toxicity.
w: Wrong - cellulitis has a flat, ill-defined margin because it is deeper.
Correct - raised, shiny, sharply demarcated plaque on the face = erysipelas.
Wrong - no pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus or shock.
Wrong - a carbuncle is a nodular abscess with multiple draining tracts.
Wrong - contact dermatitis is itchy and non-febrile, with no sharp tender raised edge.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man presents with a tender, bright red, raised plaque on the shin with a sharply demarcated margin after a small abrasion. Temperature is 37.6 °C, heart rate 88/min, BP 132/80. He has no drug allergies and can take oral medication.
What is the first-line antibiotic according to the Malaysian National Antimicrobial Guideline?
mcq.e: The sharply demarcated raised plaque indicates erysipelas, usually due to Streptococcus pyogenes, which remains sensitive to penicillin. NAG recommends cold packs, analgesia and oral penicillin V 500 mg QID, reserving IV cefuroxime 750 mg TDS for severe disease. Broad-spectrum agents are unnecessary and topical agents cannot reach the dermal lymphatics.
w: Wrong - ciprofloxacin has poor streptococcal cover.
Wrong - piperacillin-tazobactam is reserved for severe cellulitis with hypotension.
Wrong - metronidazole covers anaerobes only.
Wrong - topical therapy is for folliculitis, not dermal infection.
Correct - oral penicillin V 500 mg QID is first-line for mild erysipelas.

mcq.stem:
A 63-year-old diabetic woman has a hot, swollen, tender left leg with poorly defined erythema spreading from a heel fissure. Temperature is 39.2 °C, heart rate 124/min and BP 82/50 mmHg despite 1 L of crystalloid. There is no crepitus, bullae or pain out of proportion.
Which empirical antibiotic is most appropriate per Malaysian NAG?
mcq.e: NAG grades cellulitis by systemic involvement: mild has no systemic signs (oral cloxacillin 500 mg QID), moderate has systemic signs without hypotension (IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID), and severe has systemic signs with hypotension (IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g). Hypotension makes this severe cellulitis. Note: slide writes cloxacillin 'QOD'; the correct frequency is QID (6-hourly).
w: Correct - severe cellulitis (systemic signs + hypotension) needs IV piperacillin-tazobactam.
Wrong - oral cloxacillin is for mild cellulitis without systemic signs.
Wrong - IV cloxacillin is for moderate cellulitis without hypotension.
Wrong - IV cefuroxime is the NAG option for severe erysipelas.
Wrong - oral penicillin is for mild erysipelas.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old man has 3 days of spreading, poorly demarcated erythema and swelling of the forearm after a laceration. Temperature is 38.6 °C and heart rate 106/min; BP is 128/76 mmHg and he is alert. There is no fluctuance.
Which empirical antibiotic is most appropriate per Malaysian NAG?
mcq.e: Fever and tachycardia without hypotension classify this as moderate cellulitis, treated with IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID to cover Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes. Oral cloxacillin is for mild cellulitis without systemic features, and piperacillin-tazobactam is kept for severe cellulitis with hypotension.
w: Wrong - oral therapy is for mild cellulitis with no systemic signs.
Wrong - penicillin V lacks reliable staphylococcal cover and is for erysipelas.
Correct - systemic signs without hypotension = moderate: IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID.
Wrong - Tazocin is reserved for severe cellulitis with hypotension.
Wrong - topical agents cannot treat subcutaneous infection.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has a 6 cm indurated, very tender lesion on the nape of his neck. Pus drains from several separate openings on its surface. Temperature is 38.1 °C. Pus culture later grows Staphylococcus aureus.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Warm compresses and topical fusidic acid
Oral penicillin V with cold packs
mcq.e: Several furuncles joined together in the subcutaneous tissue, discharging through multiple tracts on the nape of the neck in a diabetic, form a carbuncle. The interconnected loculi need incision and drainage (saucerisation) together with systemic IV cloxacillin 1-2 g QID. Warm compresses and oral cloxacillin are sufficient only for simple furuncles.
w: Wrong - topical therapy is for folliculitis, far too little for a carbuncle.
Wrong - this is the erysipelas regimen and misses staphylococci.
Wrong - aspiration cannot drain multiple interconnected loculi.
Correct - carbuncle: incision and drainage (saucerisation) plus IV cloxacillin.
Wrong - oral therapy alone is inadequate for a febrile carbuncle.

mcq.stem:
A 24-year-old obese man has a 4-day history of a single, painful, red nodule about 1.5 cm across in the right axilla. It has a central yellow point and is becoming fluctuant. A week earlier he noticed small itchy papules with pustules around the hair follicles in the same area. He is afebrile.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: A furuncle (boil) is a collection of pus in the dermis or deeper around a single follicle, usually following folliculitis, at sweat and friction sites such as the axilla, neck and buttocks. Folliculitis is superficial with small pustular papules; a carbuncle is a larger subcutaneous lesion formed by several furuncles with multiple draining tracts. Treat with warm compresses, oral cloxacillin 500 mg QID for 5-7 days and drainage if fluctuant.
w: Wrong - folliculitis was the preceding stage; it is superficial without a nodule.
Wrong - a carbuncle has multiple draining tracts and is usually larger.
Wrong - erysipelas is a raised plaque, not a pointing nodule.
Correct - single deeper follicular abscess after folliculitis = furuncle.
Wrong - cellulitis is diffuse spreading erythema without a pointing abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old diabetic man has 2 days of severe left leg pain after a minor scratch. The pain is far greater than the mild erythema suggests. The calf is tense and shiny with dusky patches, bullae and crepitus. Temperature is 39 °C, BP 90/55 mmHg. CRP 250 mg/L, WCC 26 × 10^9/L, Na 128 mmol/L, glucose 22 mmol/L. IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics have been started.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: MRI of the leg to define extent
IV antibiotics and review in 24 hours
mcq.e: Pain out of proportion, bullae, dusky skin, crepitus, septic shock and a high LRINEC score indicate necrotising fasciitis. Mortality rises with every hour of delay, so after starting resuscitation and antibiotics the patient goes straight to theatre for emergent radical debridement, which also confirms the diagnosis (finger test, tissue biopsy). Imaging must not delay surgery, and there should be a low threshold for amputation if life-threatening.
w: Correct - urgent radical surgical debridement is life-saving and diagnostic.
Wrong - imaging must never delay surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis.
Wrong - antibiotics alone cannot penetrate necrotic fascia; waiting is fatal.
Wrong - this treats simple cellulitis and ignores the necrotising process.
Wrong - HBOT is at most an adjunct after debridement, never first.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old fisherman with alcoholic liver cirrhosis cut his hand while cleaning fish in seawater. Within 24 hours he has severe forearm pain, haemorrhagic bullae and hypotension. Surgical exploration shows grey necrotic fascia; Gram stain shows curved Gram-negative rods.
Which type of necrotising fasciitis is this?
mcq.e: Type 3 necrotising fasciitis is caused by marine Vibrio vulnificus, a Gram-negative rod, after seawater or seafood exposure, and is especially severe in patients with liver disease. Type 1 is polymicrobial (80-90%, diabetics and immunosuppressed), type 2 is monomicrobial group A strep in healthy people, and type 4 is fungal.
w: Wrong - type 1 is polymicrobial, typically diabetics or post-operative perineum/abdomen.
Wrong - group A strep are Gram-positive cocci in chains.
Wrong - fungal infection would show hyphae, not Gram-negative rods.
Wrong - clostridia are Gram-positive rods causing gas gangrene.
Correct - marine exposure with Gram-negative rods = type 3 (Vibrio vulnificus).

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old diabetic man has a swollen, extremely painful thigh. The registrar is calculating his LRINEC score to support a suspicion of a necrotising soft tissue infection and has ordered several blood tests.
Which of the following results is NOT part of the LRINEC score?
mcq.e: LRINEC (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotising Fasciitis) uses six tests: CRP, white cell count, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose. A score of 6 or more is suspicious and 8 or more strongly predictive. ESR is not included. A low score never excludes the diagnosis, which remains clinical and surgical.
w: Wrong - CRP is a LRINEC component (≥ 150 mg/L scores heavily).
Correct - ESR is not part of the LRINEC score.
Wrong - hyponatraemia (< 135 mmol/L) is a component.
Wrong - low haemoglobin is a component.
Wrong - raised creatinine is a component.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old previously healthy woman has necrotising fasciitis of the arm after a minor cut. Tissue culture grows Streptococcus pyogenes sensitive to penicillin. She is on high-dose IV benzylpenicillin after debridement, and the consultant insists clindamycin is continued alongside it.
What is the main reason for adding clindamycin?
mcq.e: Clindamycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and therefore shuts down production of streptococcal (and clostridial) exotoxins that drive shock and tissue necrosis. It works regardless of growth phase, whereas penicillin is less effective at high bacterial loads (Eagle effect). It is used with, not instead of, penicillin. Lecturer pearl: the toxin-suppression rationale is beyond the slides.
w: Wrong - MRSA is not the issue here and clindamycin resistance is common.
Wrong - anaerobes are irrelevant in pure streptococcal infection.
Correct - clindamycin suppresses toxin production via protein synthesis inhibition.
Wrong - clindamycin has no useful Gram-negative synergy.
Wrong - penetration is not the main reason for its use in NF.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old previously healthy footballer grazed his thigh during a match. Thirty-six hours later he has rapidly spreading, exquisitely painful swelling of the thigh, fever of 39.5 °C and hypotension. He has no diabetes, no marine exposure and no recent surgery.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
mcq.e: Type 2 necrotising fasciitis is monomicrobial, most often group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), and typically affects the limbs of young healthy people after minor trauma, often with toxic shock. Type 1 polymicrobial infection is the commonest overall but occurs in diabetics and immunosuppressed or post-operative patients. Vibrio follows marine exposure.
w: Wrong - clostridia cause gas gangrene after contaminated deep wounds.
Wrong - Vibrio requires marine or seafood exposure.
Correct - healthy young patient with limb NF = type 2, group A strep.
Wrong - Pseudomonas is not a typical NF pathogen in healthy people.
Wrong - Bacteroides is part of type 1 polymicrobial infection.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old construction worker sustains a crushed, soil-contaminated open wound of the calf. Twenty-four hours later he has severe pain, swelling, bronze discolouration with haemorrhagic blisters, and crackling on palpation. X-ray shows gas tracking along the muscle planes. He is tachycardic and confused.
Which organism is most likely responsible?
mcq.e: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) follows traumatic or surgical wounds contaminated with Clostridium species, chiefly C. perfringens, whose toxins destroy muscle and produce gas. Features are severe pain, swelling, discolouration, crepitus, haemorrhagic blisters and rapid progression with high mortality. Treatment is urgent surgical debridement or amputation plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
w: Wrong - group A strep causes type 2 NF but does not typically form gas.
Wrong - S. aureus causes abscesses and cellulitis, not gas-forming myonecrosis.
Wrong - Vibrio follows marine exposure.
Wrong - Pasteurella follows cat and dog bites.
Correct - soil-contaminated crush wound with gas in muscle = Clostridium perfringens.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old diabetic smoker has a black, dry, shrivelled fourth toe with a clear line of demarcation. There is no discharge, odour or surrounding erythema. He is afebrile and WCC is normal. ABI is 0.4 and angiography shows focal stenoses of the superficial femoral and tibial arteries.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent guillotine amputation at the ankle
Wet dressings to soften the eschar
mcq.e: Dry gangrene is ischaemic necrosis without infection; the priority is to restore blood flow by endovascular or surgical revascularisation, with antiplatelet agents, statins and blood pressure control, before any limited amputation of the demarcated toe. Wet or gas gangrene, by contrast, needs urgent debridement or amputation and broad-spectrum antibiotics. ABI below 0.9 indicates arterial insufficiency (slide quotes < 1.0).
w: Wrong - urgent major amputation is for life-threatening wet or gas gangrene.
Correct - dry gangrene: restore blood flow plus antiplatelet and statin therapy.
Wrong - there is no infection to treat.
Wrong - HBOT does not correct a proximal arterial stenosis.
Wrong - moistening dry gangrene risks converting it to wet gangrene.

mcq.stem:
A 66-year-old woman with diabetes has a black second toe whose discolouration is now spreading onto the dorsum of the foot, which is swollen, moist and foul-smelling with pus. Temperature is 39 °C and WCC 21 × 10^9/L. Dorsalis pedis pulse is weak.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Revascularisation first, then reassess in two weeks
Oral co-amoxiclav and outpatient wound review
Allow auto-amputation with dry dressings at home
Total contact cast and offloading for six weeks
mcq.e: Ischaemic tissue that has become infected is wet gangrene, common in diabetics because of impaired healing. It is a source of spreading sepsis and needs urgent surgical debridement or amputation of the infected necrotic tissue together with broad-spectrum IV antibiotics; vascular assessment follows once sepsis is controlled. Diabetics with critical limb ischaemia have up to 50% amputation or death within a year.
w: Correct - wet gangrene: urgent source control plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
Wrong - delaying source control in a septic foot risks the limb and life.
Wrong - oral outpatient therapy is inadequate for a septic patient.
Wrong - auto-amputation is only acceptable for dry, uninfected gangrene.
Wrong - casting is contraindicated in an infected ischaemic foot.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old dental nurse has a 2-day history of burning pain in the tip of her right index finger. There are clusters of small vesicles containing clear fluid on an erythematous base. The pulp is soft, not tense, and there is no pus. She had a cold sore a week ago.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Incision and drainage under digital block
