mcq.e: Clear vesicles with burning pain and a soft pulp in a healthcare worker suggest herpetic whitlow (HSV), an important differential of felon and paronychia. It is self-limiting and treated with antivirals such as acyclovir; incision is contraindicated because it can spread the virus and cause bacterial superinfection. A felon, by contrast, is a tense, throbbing pulp abscess needing drainage.
w: Wrong - incising a herpetic whitlow spreads infection and invites superinfection.
Wrong - this is a viral infection; antistaphylococcal therapy does not help.
Wrong - fish-mouth incisions are avoided even for felons.
Correct - herpetic whitlow: antiviral therapy and no incision.
Wrong - drainage incisions are for bacterial felons, not HSV.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old florist pricked the palmar aspect of her right index finger on a rose thorn 2 days ago. The finger is now painful, warm and red. You are examining for signs that indicate infection within a synovial sheath.
Which examination finding is the most specific early sign?
o: Erythema over the dorsum of the hand
mcq.e: The four Kanavel signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis are a flexed posture, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the flexor sheath and pain on passive extension. Pain on passive extension, caused by stretching the pus-filled sheath, is the earliest and most specific; fusiform swelling is the most common. Lecturer pearl: specificity ranking is beyond the slides.
w: Correct - pain on passive extension is the earliest and most specific Kanavel sign.
Wrong - fusiform swelling is the most common sign but less specific.
Wrong - flexed posture is a Kanavel sign but less specific.
Wrong - sheath tenderness is a Kanavel sign but less specific than passive-stretch pain.
Wrong - dorsal erythema is non-specific and not a Kanavel sign.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with diabetes presents 4 days after a puncture wound to the palmar middle finger. The finger is held flexed with uniform sausage-like swelling, tenderness along the whole flexor sheath and severe pain on passive extension. Temperature is 38.4 °C.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Oral co-amoxiclav and a resting splint
Ray amputation of the middle finger
mcq.e: All four Kanavel signs indicate pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis. Non-operative IV antibiotics, splintage and elevation are only for very early cases, with review within 24 hours. Late presentation (here 4 days), a diabetic host or failure to improve in 24 hours mandates operative incision, drainage and irrigation of the flexor sheath followed by culture-specific IV antibiotics, to prevent tendon necrosis, rupture and stiffness.
w: Wrong - oral outpatient treatment is inadequate for an established sheath infection.
Wrong - a 48-hour trial is too long and inappropriate for late presentation.
Wrong - supportive care alone allows tendon necrosis.
Correct - late PFFT: operative sheath drainage and irrigation plus IV antibiotics.
Wrong - amputation is not first-line for a salvageable finger.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old diabetic woman who checks her capillary glucose from her right thumb has severe throbbing pain in the thumb tip for 3 days. The pulp is tense, red and exquisitely tender with a fluctuant area; swelling stops at the distal interphalangeal flexion crease. X-ray is not required.
What is the most appropriate management?
mcq.e: A tense, fluctuant pulp abscess whose swelling stops at the DIP crease is a felon, commonly from glucometer needlesticks in diabetics. Once there is a drainable abscess, bedside incision and drainage with antibiotics is required; a lateral (midaxial) incision avoids the tactile pulp and digital neurovascular bundles, and fish-mouth incisions are avoided because of scarring and instability. Oral antibiotics alone are only for early felons without abscess.
w: Wrong - oral antibiotics alone suit only an early felon without an abscess.
Wrong - soaks and ointment are for paronychia without abscess.
Correct - drainable felon: lateral incision and drainage with antibiotics.
Wrong - fish-mouth incisions cause painful scars and an unstable pulp.
Wrong - lifting the eponychial fold drains a paronychia, not a pulp abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old fishmonger had a fish bone puncture at the base of his thumb 3 days ago. The ball of the thumb and first web space are tense and swollen, the thumb is held abducted, and thumb flexion and opposition are very painful. The dorsum of the hand is puffy. Index, middle, ring and little fingers flex without pain.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.e: Deep fascial space infections are localised by which finger movements are painful: thenar space - pain on thumb flexion with swelling of the thenar eminence and first web and an abducted thumb; hypothenar - pain on little finger flexion; midpalmar - pain on middle, ring and little finger flexion. Dorsal swelling occurs in all because the dorsal skin is lax. Treatment is incision and drainage followed by IV antibiotics.
w: Wrong - midpalmar infection causes pain on middle, ring and little finger flexion.
Wrong - hypothenar infection causes pain on little finger flexion.
Wrong - a collar-button abscess lies between two fingers and spreads them apart.
Wrong - flexor tenosynovitis gives Kanavel signs along a single digit.
Correct - painful thumb flexion with first web swelling and abducted thumb = thenar space.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old cook who washes dishes for many hours daily has had swollen, mildly tender nail folds on three fingers for 3 months. The cuticles are absent, the nail folds are thickened and boggy, and there is no pus. Nail plates show ridging.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Incision of the lateral nail fold
mcq.e: Paronychia lasting more than 6 weeks is chronic, often fungal (Candida albicans) or mixed, and linked to wet work that destroys the cuticle barrier. Management is to avoid trauma and moisture and to use topical or systemic antifungals such as itraconazole or terbinafine. Acute paronychia (under 6 weeks) is usually Staphylococcus aureus, treated with warm soaks or drainage if an abscess forms.
w: Wrong - antistaphylococcal antibiotics treat acute bacterial paronychia.
Correct - chronic paronychia: antifungals and protection from wet work and trauma.
Wrong - there is no abscess to drain.
Wrong - antivirals treat herpetic whitlow.
Wrong - soaks with antibiotic ointment suit acute paronychia without abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old intravenous drug user presented 5 days ago with an infected little finger flexor sheath and did not return. He now has a diffusely swollen, erythematous, shiny little finger AND thumb, with pain in the palm and distal forearm. The index, middle and ring fingers are spared.
Through which route has the infection most likely spread to the thumb?
o: Thenar space via the first web
Carpal tunnel along the median nerve
mcq.e: The little finger sheath continues as the ulnar bursa and the thumb (FPL) sheath as the radial bursa. These bursae communicate through Parona's space, which lies in the distal forearm between FDP and pronator quadratus, so pus in one spreads to the other, producing a horseshoe abscess. Treatment is IV antibiotics, incision and drainage (Brunner incisions) and physiotherapy. Note: slide places Parona's space in the mid-palm; it lies in the distal forearm.
w: Wrong - midpalmar spread would involve the middle and ring fingers.
Wrong - thenar space infection does not connect the little finger sheath to the thumb.
Wrong - the dorsal space does not link the flexor bursae.
Wrong - the carpal tunnel transmits the bursae but the communication occurs in Parona's space.
Correct - radial and ulnar bursae communicate via Parona's space = horseshoe abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman had a manicure 3 days ago. Her right ring finger now has a red, swollen, throbbing lateral nail fold with a collection of yellow pus visible beneath the skin, which is fluctuant. The pulp is soft and there are no vesicles.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Warm soaks and triple antibiotic ointment
Incision and drainage of the fold
Surgical removal of the whole nail
mcq.e: Acute paronychia (under 6 weeks) is usually Staphylococcus aureus entering through a breached cuticle. Without an abscess, warm soaks 5-6 times daily for 10-15 minutes with antibiotic ointment suffice, but once pus has collected the abscess must be incised and drained by elevating the nail fold. Antifungals are for chronic paronychia and antivirals for herpetic whitlow.
w: Wrong - soaks and ointment are only for paronychia without an abscess.
Correct - acute paronychia with abscess: incision and drainage.
Wrong - antifungals are for chronic (fungal) paronychia.
Wrong - antivirals treat herpetic whitlow, which has clear vesicles.
Wrong - total nail removal is excessive for a localised fold abscess.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old man says he cut his hand on a door last night. There is a 5 mm laceration over the dorsum of the right fourth metacarpophalangeal joint with swelling and pain on movement of the finger. X-ray shows no fracture or foreign body. He later admits to punching someone in the mouth.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Primary wound suture and oral cloxacillin
Steri-strips and review in one week
Formal exploration and washout in theatre
Tetanus toxoid and a dry dressing
mcq.e: A small laceration over the 3rd or 4th MCP joint from a clenched fist is a fight bite until proven otherwise. When the finger extends, the extensor tendon wound slides away and seals oral bacteria inside the joint, risking septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Management is formal surgical exploration and washout, leaving the wound open, plus amoxicillin-clavulanate covering Eikenella corrodens, staphylococci and streptococci.
w: Wrong - closing a contaminated bite traps bacteria; cloxacillin misses Eikenella.
Wrong - superficial closure ignores possible joint penetration.
Wrong - antibiotics alone do not clean a contaminated joint.
Correct - fight bite: formal exploration and washout plus co-amoxiclav.
Wrong - tetanus is needed but does not treat the joint contamination.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man presents 3 days after punching another man in the mouth, with a swollen, discharging wound over the third knuckle. Culture grows a slow-growing, fastidious Gram-negative rod that pits the agar and gives a bleach-like odour. It is resistant to clindamycin.
Which organism is this?
mcq.e: Human bite infections are polymicrobial, typically Eikenella corrodens, Staphylococcus aureus, viridans streptococci and anaerobes. Eikenella is a fastidious Gram-negative rod from human oral flora that corrodes (pits) agar; it is resistant to clindamycin and cloxacillin but sensitive to amoxicillin-clavulanate. Note: slide spells it 'Eikonella'. Lecturer pearl: laboratory features are beyond the slides.
w: Correct - human oral flora, agar-pitting Gram-negative rod = Eikenella corrodens.
Wrong - Pasteurella comes from cat and dog bites.
Wrong - Capnocytophaga follows dog bites, especially in asplenic patients.
Wrong - Vibrio follows marine exposure.
Wrong - Bartonella causes cat-scratch disease.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman was bitten on the dorsum of her hand by her own vaccinated pet cat 2 hours ago. There are two small, deep puncture wounds that have already sealed. There is no tendon injury. Her tetanus booster was 3 years ago and she has no drug allergies.
Apart from copious irrigation, which antibiotic is most appropriate?
mcq.e: Cat teeth make deep punctures that seal immediately, inoculating bacteria into deep tissue, so cat bites carry a higher infection risk than dog bites. Infections are polymicrobial with anaerobes, and Pasteurella multocida is the commonest isolate from both cats and dogs. Prophylactic amoxicillin-clavulanate covers these; cloxacillin, cephalexin and clindamycin alone have poor Pasteurella activity. Give tetanus toxoid if due, and consider rabies prophylaxis if the animal's behaviour is suspicious.
w: Wrong - cloxacillin has poor activity against Pasteurella.
Wrong - first-generation cephalosporins cover Pasteurella poorly.
Correct - amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Pasteurella and anaerobes.
Wrong - clindamycin alone misses Pasteurella.
Wrong - deep cat punctures are high-risk and warrant prophylaxis.
